THE THREE NPC MODES — ROLE-CONSISTENT BEHAVIOR, DISTRESS, RAGE

Irreverents \| Core world and NPC behavior design \| 22 November 2026

# Owner-confirmed definition

NPCs generally have THREE modes:

1. BUSINESS AS USUAL.

2. CONFUSION / DISTRESS.

3. ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE.

This applies to villains as much as to shopkeepers, guards, sages, pets and other inhabitants. These are modes of response to ROLE CONFORMITY, not moral alignment, friendliness or hostility.

Every inhabitant sincerely LOVES playing their predefined part in an almost religious Hero's Journey. They believe all people and objects have one obvious, gloriously meaningful purpose. They expect everyone else to act in typecast ways too. Deviations initially seem like temporary flukes; repeated violation causes mounting cognitive dissonance and intense distress; persistent refusal to return to script can drive even ordinary shopkeepers and pets to desperate, blinding rage. Conversely, credible return to expected behavior reassures them almost immediately. “Yup! Just as expected!”

# The single most important clarification

BUSINESS AS USUAL DOES NOT MEAN NONVIOLENCE, FRIENDSHIP, SAFETY, OR SOCIAL PEACE.

A shopkeeper defending his wares against a stereotypically villainous villain is BUSINESS AS USUAL. The shopkeeper opposes the villain out loud and may fight him, while inwardly feeling completely comfortable that all is as it should be.

A villain marauding, threatening, grandstanding or fighting a foretold champion is BUSINESS AS USUAL for the villain too. The villain is delighted to be villainous. An honorable champion defending the gate and a dragon threatening a village can all inhabit their most satisfied, stable mode in the SAME battle. Nobody experiences narrative dissonance simply because an anticipated conflict happens.

A villain casually and politely entering the shop to BUY A POTION, behaving like a well-mannered hero customer, is profoundly distressing to the shopkeeper. He would prefer the villain come to rob or terrorize him, because that would be expected. Likewise, a villain may be alarmed if a hero refuses their glorious duel and instead wants to inventory the villain's furniture.

WHO is acting matters just as much as WHAT they are doing.

# Mode 1 — BUSINESS AS USUAL

Inner experience: joyful confidence, pride, certainty that life is proceeding exactly as the glorious story requires.

External actions: role-appropriate routine, commerce, trials, heroic warnings, threats, combat, villainy, ceremonies, challenges, guarding, prophecy-giving, dragon attacks, quest rewards.

The shopkeeper beams when a hero buys a potion. He may also courageously swing his broom at a villain stealing goods while remaining inwardly fulfilled: “Exactly! This is why there are honest shopkeepers!”

The Dark Lord may laugh magnificently at a hero's attack. He is proud to be a formidable adversary. A guardsman can be comfortable enforcing a law against an ordained thief. Those confrontations are part of the expected narrative.

Game implication: business as usual does NOT mean no attack behavior; combat can be a scripted, normal routine for two opposing NPC archetypes.

# Mode 2 — CONFUSION / DISTRESS

Inner experience: this makes no sense, but it MUST be a fluke or misunderstanding; the expected order will resume in a moment.

External actions: puzzled staring, hesitation, polite correction, increasingly urgent pleading, protesting, explanation, inspection, attempted redirection, frantic efforts to restore the appropriate scene.

Example: The designated villain walks into a shop and asks, “Good afternoon! One healing potion, please.” The shopkeeper is horrified at the entirely wrong script. He may ask if this is a trick, look for the missing hero, insist the villain make a proper threat, or frantically summon someone who can clarify what to do.

Example: A hero tries to buy the shop itself, remove its roof and turn it into a wheeled battering ram. The shopkeeper loves the shop AS A SHOP and cannot understand why any hero would want it for another purpose.

Example: The Dark Lord makes his terrifying entrance. The heroes immediately inspect his throne, ask about a hidden passage, or begin experimenting with his siege engine. The villain is deeply distressed because the heroic confrontation is being ignored.

Game implication: the NPC is NOT simply more hostile in this state. They are emotionally destabilized and try to correct the script before fully losing control.

# Mode 3 — ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE

Inner experience: sustained deviation has become psychologically intolerable. The world MUST be put right.

External actions: abandon ordinary routines, scream, charge, strike, throw objects, join enormous crowds, collide with more powerful heroes, give up tactical caution. Not just guards and champions: ordinary shopkeepers, elderly customers, servants and pet cats can hurl themselves at the offenders.

This rage is not moral retribution or righteous law enforcement in disguise. It is extreme cognitive-dissonance breakdown. It can unite opposing factions who usually have prescribed antagonisms: the designated villain and a shopkeeper could both be outraged by a player who will not behave like the proper hero and, for a moment, both try to correct the player, though exact alliances need contextual design.

Ordinary noncombatants should remain mechanically ordinary and often hopeless against very strong heroes; the spectacular danger emerges from mass, unpredictable swarming, the presence of real guards and machines, chain collisions and frantic escalation.

The exact proximity, duration and participation mechanics are implementation questions. Do not lock a five-star meter or arbitrary level thresholds as canon.

# Transitions: a simple, asymmetric model

Expected behavior, whether pleasant OR hostile → BUSINESS AS USUAL.

First unexpected action → suspicion that it was a fluke; transition toward CONFUSION / DISTRESS.

Persistent inexplicable deviation → increasing distress and attempts to correct behavior.

Prolonged or intensified contradiction → ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE.

For GOOD GUYS still in mode 2 distress, a convincing return to expected behavior can quickly restore business as usual. Once they reach mode 3 violent rage, the player must disengage and stay incident-free until general alarm/heat subsides below the violent threshold; merely behaving normally in front of raging NPCs is not enough.

The script is so trusted that a brief sign of confirmation restores everyone’s confidence. “Yup! Just as expected!” The exact speed and limits when there are severe physical harms, ongoing danger or obvious evidence of a lie remain open.

These THREE modes replace the earlier proposed six-stage escalation as the OWNER-CONFIRMED high-level NPC model. Intermediate animation beats and alert levels can still be implementation details INSIDE them, not additional canonical core modes.

# The role-consistency test, NOT a good-versus-evil test

Shopkeeper sees HERO buy potion: BUSINESS AS USUAL, delighted transaction.

Shopkeeper sees VILLAIN threaten to rob stock: BUSINESS AS USUAL, proudly opposes villain.

Shopkeeper sees VILLAIN politely buy potion: CONFUSION / DISTRESS; persistent insistence could lead to RAGE.

Villain sees HERO challenge him to epic battle: BUSINESS AS USUAL, jubilant antagonism.

Villain sees HERO ignore him to inspect furniture: CONFUSION / DISTRESS, potentially escalating to RAGE.

Guard sees HERO accept rightful mission: BUSINESS AS USUAL, respectful conduct.

Guard sees HERO suplex king through stained glass: unexpected deviation → distress/rage.

Villager sees HERO slay the foretold dragon: BUSINESS AS USUAL, gratitude and celebration.

Villager sees HERO immediately steal the awarded cloak's intended town treasure: dissonance and panic → possible rage.

An NPC can be actively fighting another while in BUSINESS AS USUAL. The key is whether the opponent's conduct confirms the worldview.

# Signature vignette: a normal villain transaction

A villain bursts into a provisioner's shop.

“YOUR WARES ARE MINE, MISERABLE SHOPKEEPER!”

The shopkeeper clutches his broom in joyous determination: “NEVER, YOU VILE SCOUNDREL!” All is exactly as expected.

The villain leaves. Later he returns, removes his hat and says, “Good afternoon. Do you stock healing potions?”

The merchant freezes. “...What?”

“Sixteen gold for the larger bottle? A fair price.”

The merchant's face pales. “You... you are a VILLAIN. You are supposed to TAKE THINGS!”

If he continues smiling politely and offering exact change, the merchant's distress mounts, perhaps drawing guards and neighbors into increasingly frantic attempts to make him behave villainously.

Finally the villain knocks over a display and shouts, “ALL YOUR GOODS BELONG TO ME!”

The merchant straightens up in relief: “Ah, THERE you are, you miserable fiend!” He charges with the broom again, inwardly content.

This is an EXAMPLE of tone and mechanics, not an approved scripted mission.

# The consequences for world design

NPC role fidelity must be clear enough for players to predict. This makes shops, castles, villain lairs, temples, taverns and arenas useful gameplay grammars rather than just decorative themes.

Apparent politeness can be alarming, and violence can be reassuring, according to WHO is doing WHAT and in WHICH narrative setting. As such “friend or foe” AI is not a substitute for expectation evaluation.

Player characters gain a new form of social stealth: look and act like the kind of figure everyone expects; guards and citizens may stop questioning even a previously alarming actor.

Pursuit can be a battle against mounting disbelief, not mere criminal heat. A heroic purchase or properly staged confrontation may pacify observers faster than hiding for several minutes.

The Hall of Legends objectively records epic incidents even when most inhabitants are delighted or appalled by their narrative appropriateness.

Co-op can intensify the effect: a party member reassuring one group while another violates the expected scene in a different room; local knowledge and witness propagation remain important.

# Tone constraints

NPCs are sincerely delighted to be typecast; they do not wink at the audience or secretly yearn for a different life.

The world is not primarily oppressive. The roles are intrinsically satisfying to those who inhabit them.

People should try to explain away early deviations as flukes before rage, rather than escalating to military force on the first whimsical experiment.

Rage should be an extraordinary, frighteningly hilarious transformation—not the NPC's permanent personality.

Do not quietly reinterpret all deviations as “part of the hero's journey.” That would nullify the distress mechanism.

Keep physical damage and persistent grievances distinguishable from immediate reassurance, but avoid using them to negate the distinctive fast emotional reset.

Animals joining extreme resistance is owner-confirmed as a spectacle; exactly how they comprehend narrative roles is open.

# Prototype validation matrix

Test 1: In same shop, normal hero purchase produces delight; stereotypical villain robbery produces expected opposition WITHOUT distress; polite villain shopping produces alarm and possible rage.

Test 2: The same villain performs threatening robbery after distress and the shopkeeper visibly calms while continuing to oppose him.

Test 3: The same shopkeeper can be in BUSINESS AS USUAL and physically hostile; conflict is not conflated with dissonance.

Test 4: Repeated deviation leads from confused correction to panic and mass rage; nearby weak NPCs join without gaining unreasonable strength.

Test 5: Expected behavior rapidly reassures good-guy NPCs in mode 2, but does NOT automatically pacify mode 3. Full avoidance and a sustained incident-free cooldown are required.

Test 6: A villain and hero can each become distressed by the other's refusal to fulfill their prescribed opposing role.

Test 7: Avoid rigid one-action lookup tables where the world context supports a plausible alternative explanation or temporary fluke.

# Status and next open design questions

OWNER CONFIRMED: three modes, applicability to villains too, cheerful satisfaction in archetypal role performance, normal villainy reassuring to shopkeeper even as shopkeeper opposes villain, polite villain shopping deeply distressing, persistence of deviation leads to violent rage, fast return to normal when script restored.

PROPOSED: exact dialogue; architecture of expectation checks; global versus local spread; co-op witness handling; any villain/shopkeeper unexpected alliance; specific timing, thresholds and severity conditions. “Three NPC Modes” is a descriptive design title, not an in-world religious doctrine name.

OWNER-CONFIRMED IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINT — NO NPC AI (22 NOV 2026)

All NPC behaviors are scripted and rule-triggered, NOT AI-driven. A shopkeeper's reactions to Hero-Buy, Villain-Rob, and Villain-Buy are deliberately programmed response rules. Its three modes are simple gameplay states, not evidence of an intelligent mental simulation. Persistent violations can trigger distress and rage via authored thresholds. Normal role action can immediately reassure good-guy distress (mode 2), but violent rage (mode 3) requires evasion and an incident-free cooldown until area alarm falls below its violent threshold. Shopkeepers, villains, cats and crowd characters never need to understand the narrative, choose strategies, infer intent, or learn. Avoid referring to this system as NPC AI even in conventional game-design parlance. The owner's universal three modes and role-sensitive examples remain unchanged.

OWNER-CONFIRMED DE-ESCALATION THRESHOLD — DISTRESS REASSURABLE, VIOLENCE REQUIRES COOLDOWN (22 NOV 2026)

This overrides all earlier examples that depict good-guy NPCs instantly resetting from violent rage when a hero buys a potion, bows, or resumes an expected role.

GOOD GUYS MODE 1 — BUSINESS AS USUAL: no corrective action needed.

GOOD GUYS MODE 2 — CONFUSION/DISTRESS: can be reversed quickly by the player convincingly behaving normally according to their heroic role; the observer happily accepts that the oddity was a fluke. As already confirmed, some distressed witnesses might attempt to report; prevent the call to avoid new reinforcements.

GOOD GUYS MODE 3 — ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE: returning to normal behavior IN VIEW is insufficient. The player must FULLY DISENGAGE and AVOID the hostile good guys for a sustained period, allowing the GENERAL ALARM / WANTED PRESSURE to fall below the VIOLENT THRESHOLD. During the cooldown, do not attack anyone even in self-defense, destroy anything, or do ANYTHING unexpected; ANY further incident prevents or resets the clean cooldown. Simply refusing to attack while still being chased and visible is not enough.

Once the shared alarm falls below violent level, the lower-level reassurance rule can apply again. The exact timer, alarm scale, individual-versus-general hysteresis, and whether cooling occurs in stepped tiers or continuously remain unselected. Practical proposed implementation: one shared reported heat variable, a no-incident cooldown timer, and per-NPC 3-mode state; a locally violent unreported NPC can also need avoidance/cooldown, but cannot psychically summon distant guards without a completed signal. Separate (i) local violent NPC, (ii) report status and external reinforcements, and (iii) cooldown pressure. Preserve the owner's call-before-reinforcements rule.

This rule applies to GOOD GUYS. Bad-guy outpost threats use their physically signaled reinforcement system; do not automatically require villain enemies to be narratively distressed.

Quick illustrative scenario: hero attacks a shopkeeper. At mode 2, the player returns the item and makes a normal purchase; the merchant beams and stops trying to call. In another run the hero continues until the merchant reaches mode 3; purchasing a potion now will NOT settle the rage. The player must escape into another connected room, hide, avoid all disturbance and remain undiscovered until the alarm decreases sufficiently. If pursued guards clash with bandits, the player may hide while the two groups fight; joining that fight would extend the player's wanted cooldown. No lengthy dialogue or NPC AI needed.
